The freeze-frame showed their loose ruck, a white-shirted winger stealing the ball. “Fifteen arms, one heart,” he said, tapping the screen. “We cough up the pill because we chase it alone.” He replayed the clip ten times, each pause shorter, until the squad began calling the next pass before it happened. Then he sent them out with a single rule: every pass must hit the hands at chest height, no excuses.

They trudged onto the training paddock under low Highland cloud. Finn Callaghan, the hooker who had thrown two crooked line-outs, stayed behind to sling fifty throws at the corner flag until the dew turned to mud on his sleeves. Outside-centre Iona Gray marked the try-line with her water bottle and sprinted ten shuttles, timing herself against her phone’s stopwatch, shaving off four-tenths by dusk. No one ordered the extras; they simply turned up, pairs then groups, until the floodlights buzzed alive and moths threw themselves at the bulbs.

Match-day two arrived with the smell of wet turf and deep-fried pies. Scotland’s pack locked together like Lego: eight shoulders binding, knees low, feet still. They kept the oval for twenty-three phases, milking the clock until the stand’s roar became a hum in their ears. When the whistle went for half-time they led 14-3, yet McRae warned, “Next pint tastes better but sours quicker.” They returned, scored off a scrum, then defended their five-metre line for eight brutal minutes, repelling wave after wave with ankle-tackles that left stud-marks like braille on their calves.

The table began to tilt. A last-gasp drop goal in game three, a stolen line-out in game four, and suddenly the Scots were the side no one wanted in a quarter-final. Their bus pulled out of the car park at midnight, headlights cutting through silver rain, windows fogged by songs older than any of them.

From 2011-12 to 2014-15, the count of patients moved from one ICU to another ICU rose from 60 to 75.

During that window, the share who had to return to ICU before leaving the hospital edged down from 4.5 per cent to 4.3 per cent.

Deaths on the unit slipped from 15 per cent to 14.5 per cent, yet deaths within 30 days after leaving ICU crept up from 18.2 per cent to 18.5 per cent.

The typical ICU stay shortened by 0.3 days, falling from 2.8 to 2.5, a shift linked to faster treatments and sharper rehab plans. The female share of admissions stayed between 42.5 per cent and 43.3 per cent.

Together, these numbers show a rising tide of very sick people, tighter beds, and a harder task of keeping them alive once they step out of ICU.

They kicked off at walking speed, passes rolling harmlessly out of play, shots ballooning into row Z. Groans rolled down from the stands each time a simple five-yard ball skipped off a red boot and ran white.

Then, on twenty-seven minutes, Harry Maguire thundered in a corner so hard the net snapped upright. The stadium noise flipped like a switch; shoulders lifted, strides lengthened.

Eleven minutes later Daniel James tore after a loose clearance, left two lunging legs behind, and clipped a low finish inside the far post. Touchline arms punched the air: two-goal margin, breathing space restored.

With three minutes left the referee pointed to the spot for the visitors. A hush swallowed Old Trafford. David de Gea waited on the line, shuffled a half-step right, and batted the drive aside one-handed. The whistle followed seconds later.

Solskjær called the display “scratchy yet useful,” happy simply to pocket the victory and board the bus home. Supporters filed out exchanging cautious smiles, daring to whisper that the road form might finally be waking up.

Barry Pring, 47, had flown to Kyiv to visit the woman he had met on a dating site. Ganna Ziuzina, 27, signed the marriage register with him in Donetsk during the winter of 2007; after the ceremony they kept separate homes. On 11 February 2008 the pair marked twelve months since their wedding with dinner at the O’Panas restaurant in the city centre. CCTV timed at 23:14 shows Barry staggering across the six-lane highway outside the park, apparently looking for a taxi. A black Seat Ibiza struck him and drove on without stopping.

Traffic police filed the matter as a routine road-death until reporters from Kyiv Post and later the Daily Mail traced the widow’s internet history. Detectives in Exeter opened a murder file after Barry’s brother Michael handed over bank records showing £1.4 million moved into joint accounts. The coroner’s hearing began in 2011, then stalled while officers chased statements across two jurisdictions.

February 2017 brought a fresh verdict: Mr Justice Garnham quashed the accidental-death ruling and substituted unlawful killing. The judge said evidence “points to the wife as the architect”. Phone logs placed Ganna on the grass verge seconds before impact; she had taken out a life policy six weeks earlier. By then she had reinvented herself as Julianne Moore, teaching English in a coastal Spanish town. Extradition was refused.

Barry’s relatives circulated transcripts of blazing rows over Skype; Ganna released selfies of the pair smiling in Lanzarote. She told Surrey officers in a December 2019 taped session that she had run to help her husband and screamed until ambulances arrived. The interview ended without charge. Files passed back and forth between the CPS and Kyiv prosecutors until the spring of 2021, when both sides quietly shelved the dossier.

Barry’s name still sits on the open-case list at Scotland Yard. Ganna, now remarried, posts holiday clips from Marbella and deletes comments that mention the crash. The widower’s family keep a small plaque on the A30 near Exeter airport, where the body was flown home.

Mr Turnbull, once head of government, still wants the Crown replaced by an Australian head of state, but insists the push must bubble up from households, school halls and footy clubs, not from party rooms on Capital Hill.  
“I’ve already chaired one losing ‘yes’ campaign in 1999; I’m not signing up to run a second,” he said, recalling the night the republic question was buried under a truck-load of procedural detail.

His television interview on Sunday night shoved the issue back onto talkback radio and café tables. For twenty-five years surveys have hovered around fifty-five per cent in favour of cutting colonial ties, yet the numbers never translate into MPs fearing for their seats.

Turnbull told viewers to “make noise, wave placards, sign petitions, fill town halls—until Canberra can’t pretend the mail is anything short of a roar.”  
He then added a sober footnote: even if every box were ticked, the calendar would still need a rare conjunction of elections, prime-ministerial nerve and referendum wording sweet enough to swallow.

He promised to keep writing op-eds and turning up to rallies, but conceded he may “expire under a flag still stitched with the Union Jack.”  
Victory, he said, depends on doorstep conversations outlasting news cycles; until that slow burn shows up in polling booths, parliament will keep the question parked in the too-hard tray.

Monday’s headlines called the speech a fresh ignition switch for a debate that has spent years gathering dust in the national attic.

Arthur Cory, first-born to the late Lord Penllyn, now holds the keys to Penllyn Castle, a limestone fortress outside Cowbridge where his bloodline has lived since the 1300s. In a pantry under the north tower he noticed a cedar-lined cupboard whose latch had not been oiled in decades. Inside lay a rolled banner stiff with salt-stiffened linen; candle-wax drips, sword nicks, and mended tears mapped every journey it had ridden.

The dragon on the cloth—vermilion on white-over-green—once flew from the stern of Lord Penllyn’s converted trawler when he patrolled Cardigan Bay during the war. Later it draped the mantelpiece in his rooms at Jesus College, Oxford, where he read history and sang in Welsh until dawn. Marriage, estate taxes, and a seat in the Lords pushed the banner into darkness; the cupboard door shut in 1973.

After the funeral Arthur lifted the roll, wiped off grey dust, and felt the snap of linen as it opened like a sail catching wind. Colours held: coch still bright as rowan berries, gwyrdd sharp as grass after rain. He spread it across the oak table where estate books lay open for lambing tallies. Aunt Mabel, ninety-four and living in the gatehouse, told him the flag had wrapped his father the night he was born during the blizzard of 1921. She remembered Lord Penllyn marching through Aberystwyth with the banner hoisted on a broomstick after Wales beat England at rugby in 1953.

Arthur traced a burn hole near the hoist; Mabel said a spark from a bonfire on the castle lawn had caused it the night they sang “Myfanwy” until the moon set. He telephoned three of his father’s crewmates from the coastal patrol; each recalled the same detail: when the sonar pinged a U-boat, Lord Penllyn tied the flag to the jackstaff so the dragon faced seaward. They laughed at the memory of German shells punching the water while the dragon kept flying.

That evening Arthur carried the banner upstairs to the nursery where his twins slept. He folded it small enough to fit the old pine chest that once held lead soldiers. When the boys wake, he will show them the dragon and teach them the chorus their grandfather belted out after every try.

Worldwide, physicians and nurses warn that when toddlers with asthma wait three months for inhalers, or when depressed teens wait a year for therapy, the same pattern repeats: ambulance rides, ICU beds, and coroner reports. Psychiatry wards, oncology clinics, and cardiology corridors all echo the story.

A melanoma spotted at 0.5 mm depth can be scraped away under local anaesthetic; left until bleeding, it demands a 12-hour flap surgery and months of immunotherapy. A teenager who speaks about suicidal thoughts on Monday can be offered six sessions of cognitive-behavioural therapy by Friday; if the only appointment available is in six months, the next contact may arrive in a body bag.

Japan’s rail companies record 600 suicides each year on one line alone; 70 % of those people had never seen a psychiatrist. In rural Kentucky, miners with black-lung wait until breath stops before driving two hours to the nearest pulmonologist; by then, oxygen tanks are permanent companions.

AI dermatology apps now flag suspicious moles with 95 % accuracy, and a £30 smartwatch can detect atrial fibrillation. Yet Glasgow’s homeless still queue overnight for a single GP who works Tuesdays; pregnant women in northern Nigeria cross 80 km of Boko Haram territory for a single ultrasound.

Every postponed biopsy adds £48 000 to the bill: three CT scans, six cycles of Pembrolizumab, two ambulance transfers, one palliative-care nurse for six weeks. The same cash could fund 1 200 children’s eye exams and glasses for 300 who cannot read the board.

Parliamentarians who fund fighter jets at £15 billion yet freeze health visitor posts for three years should tour a paediatric oncology ward and explain to parents why the ward runs on donated toys. Until district nurses can reach every farmhouse by 9 a.m. and school counsellors hold a 1:250 ratio, waiting lists will keep writing death certificates.

Shift one quarter of the beer advertising budget to radio spots that teach grandparents to check moles; refurbish closed high-street shops into walk-in centres open weekends; pay retention bonuses so that Dumfries keeps its senior midwife instead of watching her emigrate to Alberta. When a 60-year-old fisherman gets blood-pressure pills the day his reading hits 160/100, he stays at sea instead of occupying a stroke-rehab bed for 11 weeks.

Found by chance in 2005, the timber fish-weir off Southampton’s southern shore now lets researchers map how early settlers ate, traded, and organised labour. Rows of sharpened oak and ash poles still stand upright in the silt, once funnelled fish into a V-shaped corral every ebb tide.

Marine archaeologists rarely meet wood that has neither rotted nor drifted away. Here, two metres of estuary mud sealed the stakes from shipworm, salt, and winter gales, so axe-marks and rope-grooves survive as if cut last year. Radiocarbon runs place the felling of the trees between 690 and 720 AD; tool-waste nearby matches Saxon iron adzes.

Bone fragments wedged between the poles show spring runs of Atlantic salmon and sea-trout supplied most of the animal protein for a settlement barely three kilometres upstream. Charred vertebrae in nearby hearth middens confirm the catch was smoked, not salted, hinting at short supply chains.

Once recording and conservation finish next summer, the city will clear a tidal walkway above the stakes, letting visitors watch laser-scans appear on phone screens while water laps round the wood. Ticket sales will fund further dives.

Guides already run dawn kayak trips: paddlers read tide tables copied from Saxon reeds, then haul a replica willow trap. The trips sold out within a week of listing.

Chemists hunt for ancient DNA in the slime, engineers model how the fence altered currents, and linguists trace the lost word “*heorot-fisc” recorded for grey trout in a 9th-century charter. Each stake is a data point, each gap a question the river still answers at every low water.

The Royal Automobile Club, Britain’s oldest motoring club, told members that two separate shocks have slammed household budgets at once. Brent crude climbing above 85 dollars a barrel has lifted wholesale petrol, diesel and jet kerosene by matching margins. Sterling’s slide after the 2016 referendum has added roughly twelve cents to every dollar-denominated litre landed at Grimsby, Immingham and Thamesport. Together, the twin lifts have pushed pump prices to 148 pence for unleaded and 151 for diesel, levels last seen in autumn 2013.

Forecourt receipts rose week-on-week through October and November; the RAC’s fuel-watch team sees no ceiling while OPEC keeps supply tight and Westminster wrangles over import rules. A four-person family now spends an extra 24 pounds a month on a 55-litre tank refill compared with July; courier firms report a 17 per cent jump in their largest running cost. Covid-era savings buffers, already thin, are draining faster in counties where public transport options finish at dusk.

Chancellor Hunt received a formal plea before the November statement: trim the 53 pence per litre duty by 5 pence and scrap the 20 per cent VAT on the duty itself, a move that would shave 6 pounds off a tank. The club’s briefing paper also asked for an autumn statement clause that would tie fuel tax to the sterling-dollar rate, softening any future currency jolt.

Drivers can blunt the pain without waiting for Whitehall, the RAC added. A 2022-plate hybrid on 60 miles per gallon burns 30 per cent less liquid energy than a 2019-plate pure-combustion car returning 42; ditching roof boxes and keeping tyres at maximum sidewall pressure can slice another 7 per cent. For urban trips under five miles, folding bikes and e-scooters already cut weekly mileage for 1.3 million commuters.

Iffley Academy, which teaches 8- to 18-year-olds with special needs, will drop the initials ISIS after the terror group launched its own “Isis Academy” media wing last week. Governors feared the shared label could expose pupils to abuse or hoax calls.

Headteacher Kay Willett told reporters: “Our duty is to shield the children and staff. Sharing a name with terrorists invites threat and mix-ups we can erase with one stroke.”

The site sits on Iffley Turn, so the geographic fix was obvious. After a four-week survey, 94 % of parents, pupils and neighbours backed the switch.

Councillor John Howson, education lead at Oxfordshire County Council, praised the board: “No school should face this dilemma, yet the governors put pupil safety first.”

Willett promised lessons, therapies and admissions rules stay intact. “Nothing changes in classrooms; we keep the same badge, tie and motto—only the heading on letters will read Iffley Academy.”

Mothers and fathers greeted the news with applause at Tuesday’s coffee morning. Letterheads, website banners and signage will swap over during the summer break; email addresses change on 1 September.

Sir Nicholas Winton, a London stockbroker, scrapped his Swiss ski trip in December 1938 after a phone call from Prague. He boarded the next train to Czechoslovakia carrying only a suitcase and a list of names supplied by Doreen Warriner’s refugee committee.

Prague’s railway station teemed with parents clutching toddlers and worn envelopes stamped with exit permits. Nazi troops had swallowed the Sudetenland three months earlier; now the capital waited for the rest of the country to vanish. Parents pressed photographs into Winton’s pockets, whispering train schedules and British addresses they had never seen.

Inside a rented room above Wenceslas Square, Winton spread city maps across the floor. He matched each child to a departure date, a berth on the Harwich ferry, and a foster home scraped from synagogue noticeboards and Rotary Club newsletters. By day he queued at the British consulate for £50 guarantor bonds; by night he typed transit cards on a borrowed typewriter whose ‘e’ key kept sticking.

On 14 March 1939, the first group—twenty boys in wool caps, one girl clutching a porcelain dog—left Wilson Station at dawn. Winton knelt to tighten their shoelaces, then stayed on the platform until the locomotive smoke thinned. Nine more trains followed before Hitler closed the borders on 1 September. The final departure carried 251 children and one suitcase labeled “Handle kindly—toys inside.”

In London, Winton stored forged travel permits beneath tins of flour in his Maida Vale flat. He bribed a Dover customs officer with Players cigarettes, then convinced Home Office clerk Beatrice Wellington to stamp visas after hours. When bombs shattered Liverpool Street Station in 1940, he rerouted evacuee trains through Cambridge and wired foster families from a post-office kiosk: “Child arriving 3 p.m. Name sewn in coat.”

After the war he sold typewriter ribbons, coached Sunday football, and never mentioned Prague. In 1988 Grete Winton handed her husband a dusty scrapbook while clearing the attic; inside were 802 photographs, a page for each child, plus a pressed snowdrop from the platform. That evening BBC’s *That’s Life* host Esther Rantzen showed the album on live television. A woman in the studio audience stood up, pointed to a picture, and said, “That’s me, 1939. Thank you, Nicky.”

Marshall met a dipping cross at fifteen minutes, forehead smashing net-seeking leather to lift 11,204 throats into one booming roar. Johnson doubled the tally seven minutes later, steering a low shot inside the far post after Rovers’ centre-backs hesitated over a loose clearance.

Half-time tea had barely cooled before the script flipped. Taylor jogged out early, laces already undone, and began tormenting the left channel. On 49:58 he darted between two markers, clipped the ball off the inside of the post, and ripped his shirt over his head toward the travelling enclosure.

Smith and Young answered with a wall-pass carved through a square back line, Young side-footing under the keeper at 57’. Taylor replied instantly, collecting on the turn, riding a sliding lunge, and chipping into the roofed corner. 3-2.

Both benches threw on fresh calves; tackles snapped like dry sticks. In the 89th minute Taylor peeled to the back stick, cushioned a diagonal ball, spun, and lashed left-footed past the keeper’s despairing claw. 3-3.

The scoreboard froze, the Dons’ winless home run stretched to ten, yet every seat had stood for the last quarter-hour.

Ivory Coast’s GDP may be climbing faster than any other in the region, yet anyone trying to launch a company here still slams into a concrete wall: money is almost impossible to borrow.  
Local bankers treat a one-page business plan like a contagious disease, so founders scrape together CFA francs from cousins, corner-stall profits, or by selling their own motorbikes. These scraps keep the lights on for a month or two, never long enough to buy inventory in bulk, hire beyond two people, or reach customers outside Abidjan.

Schools teach accounting by chalkboard, not by doing. A hairdresser who opens a salon in Treichville learns pricing by losing clients to the cheaper stall next door; she records sales in a notebook whose pages tear when the fan splashes water during the daily blackout. No curriculum shows her how to forecast demand for wedding braids in October or how to read a cash-flow chart.

Inside the Plateau district, a telecom engineer turned angel investor now wires $5 000 batches to five teams every quarter through a WhatsApp pitch contest. In Bingerville, a cocoa cooperative runs weekend boot camps where 19-year-olds practice mock salary negotiations under a mango tree. Civil servants in the Ministère du Commerce have sliced the stamp-duty stack from nine sheets to four, replacing two ink signatures with a QR code.

These scattered sparks do not yet add up to a fire. Seed checks still top out at the price of a used Toyota, tariff forms swallow entire mornings, and only one incubator building offers 24-hour electricity. Until parliament releases a tax holiday clause capped specifically at firms under three years old, and until commercial banks accept warehouse receipts as collateral, the country’s growth curve will keep climbing without its own startups riding it.

Charter Communications and Cox Communications are discussing a tie-up that could redraw the map of wired internet and video in the United States.  

A single firm would replace the two rivals that now chase the same households with discounted bundles. One fewer logo on billboards means subscribers would pick from a shorter menu.  

Charter, bulked up with Cox’s 7 million accounts, would sit just behind Comcast’s 21 million, giving it the heft to squeeze programmers for lower fees and to muscle for must-carry terms.  

Opponents predict monthly bills will climb, outage response times will stretch, and niche channels could vanish once the bargaining table shrinks.  

Suppliers counter that folding duplicate call centers and fiber routes would free cash to lay 10-gig lines past 5 million extra homes and to upgrade aging nodes to DOCSIS 4.0.  

Staff lawyers at the Federal Communications Commission and the Department of Justice are now pulling subscriber data, speed tests, and pricing histories to weigh whether the swap hurts the public. Their verdict will either bless the deal or send both cable giants back to separate corners.
